name: Bleaching body hair

lead: Bleaching body hair lightens dark hair so it is less noticeable, without removing it. It is discussed as an alternative to shaving or waxing.
No studies specific to body-hair bleaching in men were found.

paras: Peroxide- and persulfate-based products oxidize and break down melanin, the pigment in hair, lightening it progressively.
Documented harms of hair bleaching products include irritant and allergic dermatitis, hives and chemical burns when misapplied; persulfates can also trigger respiratory symptoms.

lead: Bleaching body hair is the practice of lightening dark body hair with an oxidizing cosmetic product so that it is less visible, as an alternative to removing it. Hair bleaching works by oxidation breaking down melanin, typically using hydrogen peroxide with persulfate salts and an alkaline agent.[1]

Encyclopedic sources discuss bleaching mostly for scalp hair and, for body hair, mainly on women's facial hair; no studies specific to male body-hair bleaching were found.[1][2] Documented risks include irritant and allergic skin reactions and, if misapplied, chemical burns.[1]
infobox: Lightening dark body hair rather than removing it
Until hair regrows or is cut

paras: Bleaching lightens hair gradually; dark hair passes through brown, red, orange and yellow shades before reaching pale yellow, and toners are sometimes used to adjust brassy tones.[1] Home products usually contain around 6% hydrogen peroxide, while salon products can reach 9%.[1] Wikipedia mentions bleaching of body hair only in passing, as a way for women to make darker vellus hair on the upper lip less noticeable.[2]

The Wikipedia article on hair bleaching states that products can cause severe burns when applied incorrectly or left on too long, that persulfates can cause contact dermatitis, hives and swelling, and that they can provoke respiratory symptoms such as rhinitis and asthma.[1] Household sodium hypochlorite bleach is not used on hair because it damages hair structure and can chemically burn skin.[1] Skin on the body may differ from scalp skin in sensitivity, but no source consulted addressed this directly.

The practice is presented in community discussion as a middle path between visible hair and shaving: lighter hair is less noticeable while avoiding stubble and ingrown hairs. Bodybuilders and athletes who remove hair do so to highlight muscle definition or reduce friction.[2] No community threads suitable for citation were available.
